Keep the three arrows from crossing: place the Client at the left, the Metadata service above the middle, and the Storage targets at the lower right so the step 2 return arrow runs under the step 1 arrow. Side box at the top right, dashed outline with no arrows: Management service, labelled mgmtd, with the note keeps the list of nodes and targets so clients and servers can find one another. Under the Storage targets box, a small grey note: each target is a local file system on a storage server. Orange tag on step 2 only, the single most important item: the stripe pattern is set before any chunk moves. No takeaway bar.
alt: BeeGFS write: the client creates the file on metadata, which records the stripe pattern, then sends chunks to storage targets.
cap: In a BeeGFS write, the metadata service records the stripe pattern first, and the client then sends chunks to the storage targets named in that plan.

name: h20-gds-bounce-vs-direct
title: Buffered reads bounce through host DRAM, GPUDirect Storage skips it
spec: A title line at the top: one 100.0 GB read into GPU memory. Two horizontal rows, one above the other, each with a short row title on its left. Top row title: Legacy buffered I/O path. Its boxes from left to right: NVMe or storage NIC, then Host DRAM page cache, then User-space CPU buffer, then GPU HBM. Between the first box and the page cache, a short arrow labelled PCIe crossing 1. Between the user-space buffer and GPU HBM, a short arrow labelled cudaMemcpyHostToDevice, PCIe crossing 2. Between the page cache and the user-space buffer, an arrow labelled CPU copy. Under the top row, a label: 2 PCIe crossings and 200.0 GB of host DRAM read and write traffic. The Host DRAM page cache box is the orange highlight, labelled bounce buffer. Bottom row title: GPUDirect Storage path. Its boxes from left to right: NVMe or storage NIC, then GPU HBM (BAR1). One arrow between them labelled peer-to-peer DMA via cuFileRead, one PCIe crossing. A small box above the arrow labelled nvidia-fs.ko loaded. Under the bottom row, a label: 1 PCIe crossing and 0.0 GB of host DRAM bounce traffic. Keep the host DRAM box absent from the bottom row, so the difference is visible by omission. Icons: a disk cylinder for NVMe, a network port for the storage NIC, a memory chip for host DRAM, a chip for the GPU, a window for the user-space buffer. No takeaway bar.
anchor: ### 8.1 The AI data path: GPUDirect Storage (`GDS`) and NVMe staging (Volume 15)
alt: A buffered read crosses PCIe twice through host DRAM, while GPUDirect Storage moves data once with no host DRAM bounce.
cap: A buffered read crosses PCIe twice and bounces through host DRAM, while GPUDirect Storage moves the data once without touching host DRAM.

name: h20-ec-efficiency-bars
title: Usable capacity: data pieces divided by all pieces
spec: A title line at the top, then the formula line: Efficiency = D / (D + P), where D is data pieces and P is parity pieces. Below, a horizontal axis from 0% to 100% with tick marks at 0, 50, 100. Four horizontal bars stacked one above another, each with a label on the left and a percentage at the bar's end. Bar 1: 1+1 RAID-1 or buddy mirroring, 50.0%. Bar 2: 8+2 RAID-6 or EC, 80.0%. Bar 3: 16+2 distributed EC, 88.89%. Bar 4: 146+4 VAST-style wide EC, 97.33%. Bar lengths are drawn to scale against the 0% to 100% axis. Each bar has a green fill, and the 8+2 bar is the one with the orange outline, labelled example: 8 data pieces and 2 parity pieces, so 8 of every 10 pieces are useful data. Under the bars, a plain note: wider stripes keep more of the capacity usable, while a single stripe of 1+1 keeps only half. No takeaway bar.
anchor: ## 5. WEKA (WekaFS) and other distributed filesystems (*Supercomputers for Linux Sysadmins* Chapter 9)
alt: Usable capacity bars: 1+1 mirror 50 percent, 8+2 erasure coding 80 percent, 16+2 88.89 percent, 146+4 97.33 percent.
cap: Wider erasure-coded stripes keep more of the raw capacity usable than a simple mirror does.

name: h21-collective-buffer
title: Collective buffering: many small writes become a few large aligned ones
spec: Two side-by-side panels, each with a title. Left panel title: Independent writes. Draw four small boxes labelled rank stacked on the left, each with a few short arrows fanning out to a long bar labelled shared file. The arrows are many, short and scattered across the bar, drawn as small jagged marks, so the picture looks busy. Under the left panel, a grey label: many small noncontiguous requests. Right panel title: Collective buffering, two-phase I/O. Same four small boxes labelled rank on the left. Step 1 arrows, labelled exchange over the fabric, run from each rank box to two aggregator boxes in the middle, each labelled aggregator rank with the small text cb_nodes. Step 2 arrows, labelled large contiguous, stripe-aligned writes, run from each aggregator box to the long bar labelled shared file, which is drawn split into a few wide blocks with stripe boundary marks between them. Number circles 1 and 2 mark the two phases in time order. Arrows must not cross: place the ranks in one column, the aggregators in the middle column, and the file bar at the right. Orange highlight on the wide stripe-aligned blocks in the right panel, labelled the single most important item: few large writes. Under the right panel, a grey label: many small noncontiguous requests become a few large ones. No takeaway bar.
anchor: ## 1. Parallel I/O in HPC: MPI-IO and HDF5
alt: Independent writes scatter many small requests, while collective buffering gathers data on aggregators that write large aligned blocks.
cap: Collective buffering gathers data onto a few aggregator ranks, which then write large stripe-aligned blocks instead of many small scattered writes.

name: h21-dcp-reshard
title: Save on four ranks, load on two and one without rewriting the shards
spec: A title line at the top. Left column titled Save with 4 ranks. Four stacked file boxes labelled __0_0.distcp, __1_0.distcp, __2_0.distcp and __3_0.distcp, each with a small note shard (2, 3) per rank, drawn as a stack that reads as one group. Below them a separate box labelled .metadata, with the note records which slice of which tensor lives where. Draw the four shard files as one group container, labelled shard files. Right column, upper panel titled load with 2 ranks: two boxes, each labelled loaded shard (4, 3), each with the text reassembled_equal=True. Right column, lower panel titled load with 1 rank: one wide box labelled loaded shard (8, 3) with the text reassembled_equal=True. Arrows: from the group container of shard files, one arrow to the upper panel and one arrow to the lower panel, each labelled reads only the slices each rank needs. From the .metadata box, one arrow to the right column, labelled tells each rank where its slices are. The two right-column arrows must not cross the left column. Orange note on the shard files group, the single most important item: the shard files are never rewritten. Under the whole figure, a plain note: the number of ranks can change between save and load. No takeaway bar.
alt: A checkpoint saved as four shard files and a metadata file is loaded back onto two ranks and onto one rank.
cap: A distributed checkpoint saved from four ranks can be loaded onto two or one rank because the metadata records where each slice lives.

name: h21-commit-protocol
title: The crash-safe commit: five steps, then a restart that scans and verifies
spec: A left-to-right row of five numbered step cards connected by arrows, number circles 1 to 5 in time order. Step 1, title: Write shards to a temporary directory. Label: each rank writes its shards into step-N.tmp and calls fsync on them. Icon: a disk cylinder. Step 2, title: Record the manifest. Label: the coordinator writes a SHA-256 digest for each shard into MANIFEST.json, then calls fsync on it. Icon: a fingerprint or a document. Step 3, title: Rename atomically. Label: step-N.tmp becomes step-N, then the parent directory is fsynced. Icon: a tag or an arrow. Step 4, title: Move the latest pointer. Label: write a temp file, then rename it over latest. Icon: a pointer or flag. Step 5, title: Restart and verify. Label: scan for the newest step directory whose manifest and shard hashes verify. Icon: a magnifier or a shield. Below the row, a second band titled What a crash leaves behind, with three small cards in a row, each linked by a thin line back to the step where it happens. Card A, crash before rename: only a step-N.tmp directory is left, and readers ignore it, so latest stays on the last good step. Card B, crash before latest: latest is stale, and the scan finds the newer step-300 directory. Card C, corrupted shard after a commit: the hash check fails, so the loader falls back to the previous valid step. Orange highlight on step 5, labelled the single most important item: latest is a hint, the manifest and hashes are the truth. No takeaway bar.
alt: Five-step crash-safe commit: temporary write, manifest, atomic rename, latest pointer, and a verified restart scan.
cap: The commit writes to a temporary directory, renames it atomically, and on restart trusts only directories whose hashes verify.

name: h21-loader-overlap
title: Overlap: copy batch N+1 to the GPU while the GPU computes batch N
spec: A title line at the top. Three horizontal swimlanes stacked one above another, each with a lane title on its left: Loader workers, Copy stream, Compute stream. Time runs left to right with a time arrow along the bottom. In the Loader workers lane, two green blocks in sequence: prepare batch N+1, then prepare batch N+2, each block drawn above the compute block it overlaps. In the Copy stream lane, two green blocks: copy batch N+1 to GPU, labelled non_blocking, then copy batch N+2 to GPU, drawn under the compute blocks they overlap. In the Compute stream lane, two green blocks: compute batch N, then compute batch N+1. The blocks in the three lanes must line up so that the loader and copy blocks sit under the compute block of the previous batch: prepare batch N+1 and copy batch N+1 both sit under compute batch N. A small handshake marker, a grey vertical tick labelled wait_stream, sits at the start of each compute block, linked to its copy block. Orange highlight on the wait_stream handshake, labelled the single most important item: compute waits only for its own copy. Under the lanes, a grey note: if the overlap is missing, the GPU goes idle at the start of every iteration, shown as a short hatched gap at the start of a compute block. No takeaway bar.
alt: Loader and copy stream prepare the next batch while the GPU computes the current one, with a wait_stream handshake.
cap: Prefetching and a separate copy stream let the next batch move to the GPU while the current batch computes.

name: h22-ipxe-handshake
title: iPXE chain-load: the second DHCP request carries option 175
spec: A sequence diagram drawn as four vertical swimlanes side by side, each lane headed by its participant name: Node firmware (PXE ROM), iPXE program, DHCP and TFTP server, HTTP server. Messages are horizontal arrows from the sender's lane to the receiver's lane, in top-to-bottom time order, each arrow labelled with its text and numbered with a small step number. Message 1, from Node firmware to DHCP and TFTP server, labelled first DHCP request, no option 175. Message 2, from DHCP and TFTP server back to Node firmware, labelled reply with boot file ipxe.efi (UEFI) or undionly.kpxe (BIOS). Message 3, from Node firmware to DHCP and TFTP server, labelled fetch the boot file over TFTP. Message 4, from DHCP and TFTP server back to Node firmware, labelled iPXE program arrives. Message 5, from iPXE program to DHCP and TFTP server, labelled second DHCP request, option 175 set, tag ipxe. Message 6, from DHCP and TFTP server back to iPXE program, labelled reply with an HTTP URL to boot.ipxe, not another binary. Orange highlight on message 6, the single most important item, with the small note this breaks the loop. Message 7, from iPXE program to HTTP server, labelled fetch boot.ipxe script over HTTP. Keep the lanes in this order so no arrow crosses another arrow. No takeaway bar.
alt: The node boots iPXE over TFTP, then iPXE sends a second DHCP request with option 175 and receives an HTTP script URL.
cap: iPXE sends a second DHCP request with option 175, so the server answers with a script URL instead of loading iPXE again.

name: h22-stateless-layers
title: A stateless node: a read-only image in RAM, writes go to a layer above it
spec: A vertical stack of three wide layer boxes in the centre, read from bottom to top. Bottom layer, labelled Read-only image: rootfs.squashfs, downloaded into RAM at every boot, with a lock icon and the note never changes. Middle layer, labelled Writable layer: tmpfs or overlayfs, with a window or layers icon and the note every write lands here. Top layer, labelled Running node: systemd and the jobs, with a gear icon. Arrows: a single upward arrow between the layers, labelled reboot returns the node to the clean image, drawn on the right side as a return path from the top layer down to the bottom layer, not crossing the boxes. To the right of the stack, a separate column, titled Per-node identity, injected at first boot: a grey box listing SSH host keys, machine-id, hostname, Munge key, credentials, with a shield icon, and one arrow into the running node labelled injected from the provisioning server or a secret store. The identity box must not sit inside the shared image; draw it outside the stack with a dashed outline and the note not in the shared image. Below the stack, a dashed box titled Hybrid option: local NVMe for scratch, logs and container layers, with a disk cylinder icon and one arrow into the running node. Orange highlight on the reboot return path, labelled the single most important item: a reboot is a clean state. No takeaway bar.
alt: A stateless node runs a read-only squashfs image with a writable tmpfs or overlayfs layer, while identity is injected per node at first boot.
cap: A stateless node runs from a read-only image in RAM, so a reboot returns it to a clean state, and per-node identity is injected at boot.

name: h22-dtb-triage
title: Boot triage: check D, T, B and I in order and stop at the first failure
spec: A title line at the top. A left-to-right row of four stage cards connected by arrows, number circles 1 to 4 in time order. Card 1, large letter D, title DHCP, question: Did the node get an address and the right boot information? Icon: a network port. Card 2, large letter T, title Transfer, question: Did the bootloader download? Icon: a download arrow into a box. Card 3, large letter B, title Boot-mode, question: Does the binary match the firmware? Icon: a chip with a UEFI or BIOS label. Card 4, large letter I, title Image, question: Did kernel, initramfs and root load and start the OS? Icon: a window or a terminal. Under each card, one short grey check line: card 1, tcpdump port 67 or port 68 and the DHCP server logs; card 2, tcpdump port 69, the server log and the HTTP status codes; card 3, ipxe.efi versus undionly.kpxe, x86_64 versus ARM64 and Secure Boot shim; card 4, serial console output, the rd.break initramfs shell and a missing NIC driver. Under the row, a decision band with a red-free stop rule drawn as an orange bar: stop at the first failing stage. Below that, a small grey note: if the node never got its boot file name, the image stage is irrelevant. Keep card text sized so each line wraps inside its card with padding. No takeaway bar.
alt: Boot triage walks four stages in order, DHCP, Transfer, Boot-mode and Image, and stops at the first one that fails.
cap: Boot triage checks DHCP, transfer, boot mode and image in that order, and the first failing stage is where you start the fix.

name: h23-statelite-flow
title: A statelite xCAT build: six steps from media to booted nodes
spec: Six numbered step cards arranged in two rows of three, read left to right then down to the second row, with a thin arrow linking each card to the next, and number circles 1 to 6 in time order. Row one. Step 1, title: Import media and define nodes. Monospace label: copycds, then mkdef node[1-100]. Icon: a disk or a DVD. Step 2, title: Assign addresses with a regex rule. Monospace label: chtab on hosts.ip. Icon: a network address. Step 3, title: Build the statelite image. Monospace label: genimage, then chdef compute provmethod. Icon: a box or a package. Row two. Step 4, title: Set writable RAM paths. Plain label: the NFS root is read-only, so each litefile path gets writable tmpfs space in RAM. Note at least 15 entries. Icon: a sticky note. Step 5, title: Inject keys and accounts, then pack. Monospace label: add_ssh, add_passwd, liteimg. Icon: a key. Step 6, title: Generate services and boot. Monospace label: makehosts, makedhcp, makedns, nodeset, rpower node[1-100] boot. Icon: a power symbol. Orange highlight on step 5, labelled the single most important item: skip it and the nodes boot without keys and accounts. Under the figure, one grey line: the steps follow the xCAT recipe and each step depends on the one before. No takeaway bar.
anchor: #### Loading and Controlling: Step-by-step `statelite` provisioning workflow (Chapters 26 and 28)
alt: A six-step xCAT statelite build: import media, define nodes, build the image, set writable paths, inject keys, then boot.
cap: A statelite xCAT build runs from media import and node definitions through the image and its writable paths to the boot, in that order.

name: h23-bcm-image-flow
title: BCM image flow: the head copy reaches every node, and each node returns to the known good state
spec: A top-down flow. At the top, a wide box labelled Head node, with a stack icon, containing two smaller items: software image at /cm/images/<image>, and CMDaemon. Arrow down labelled updateprovisioners, with the note pushes head-copy changes to provisioning nodes. Middle row, a box labelled Provisioning nodes, which serve images to other nodes. Arrow down labelled serves the category's software image. Bottom row, two side-by-side boxes for node types, each linked from the provisioning nodes with one arrow. Left bottom box titled Diskless node: the image is copied into memory, tmpfs, shown as a small box inside a RAM icon. Right bottom box titled Diskful node: local disk contents are checked against the image, and any differing content is corrected, shown as a disk icon with a check mark. A side note box, not connected by an arrow, in the top-right: Category groups nodes and sets their software image. Another side note in the top-left above the head node box: Node installer, an early boot phase that identifies the node, partitions the disks and syncs the image, then hands over to the OS. Orange highlight on the diskful box's correction step, labelled the single most important item: drift is corrected at boot. Green takeaway bar at the bottom, one sentence from the source: a node that reboots checks itself against the image, so differences are corrected. Keep all arrows orthogonal and avoid crossings.
alt: BCM head node pushes the software image to provisioning nodes, which serve diskless and diskful compute nodes.
cap: In BCM, the head node's software image reaches each compute node through provisioning nodes, and each node is corrected to match it at boot.

name: h23-warewulf-overlays
title: Warewulf overlays: templates rendered per node, applied at two times
spec: A left-to-right layout. Left box: Container image, a chroot tree drawn as a stack of layers, labelled image unchanged by overlays. Left-middle box: Overlay, a folder of files and .ww templates. Middle box: nodes.conf, labelled per-node attributes, drawn as a table card with rows of node name, IP and image. An arrow from nodes.conf into the overlay box, labelled renders each template for each node. A right-middle box: Rendered files for one node, with the sub-label one file per template. Arrow from the overlay to rendered files. Arrows from the image and the rendered files converge into a single node box at the far right, labelled node filesystem. Two timing lanes beneath the node box: a lane labelled System overlays with the text applied once during early boot, on initramfs, and a lane labelled Runtime overlays with the text fetched and applied periodically while the node runs. A dashed callout from the node box: wwctl overlay blame <node> shows which overlay contributed each file. Orange highlight on the template rendering arrow, labelled the single most important item: the node record becomes the source for each file. No takeaway bar.
alt: Warewulf overlays are .ww templates rendered from nodes.conf for each node and applied at early boot and at runtime.
cap: Warewulf renders overlay templates from each node's record, and applies the result over the image at boot and while the node runs.

name: h24-lookup-path
title: A user lookup on a node: local files first, then the SSSD cache, and LDAP only on a miss
spec: A left-to-right flow. Left box: Lookup, with the monospace text id alice or getent passwd alice, icon: a terminal window. Arrow to a box titled nsswitch.conf, with monospace text passwd: files sss, icon: a gear. From it, a first branch to a box titled files, the local /etc/passwd file, icon: a document. If the name is found there, a short arrow to a green answer box titled Answer. Second branch from nsswitch.conf to a box titled sss, SSSD, icon: a shield. From SSSD, a decision diamond titled cache hit? Yes branch goes to the Answer box, labelled from cache, entry_cache_timeout 5400 s. No branch goes down to a box titled LDAP over ldaps://, with the failover note ldap1 and ldap2, icon: a clock or a server. From LDAP, an arrow back up to SSSD labelled stored in cache, then to Answer. A small grey note beside SSSD: enumerate = false, so SSSD looks up one name and never lists the whole directory. Orange highlight on the nsswitch.conf order arrow, labelled the single most important item: if the order is reversed, the directory is asked first for every lookup. Keep all arrows orthogonal and no arrow crosses another. No takeaway bar.
anchor: ## 4. SSSD, nsswitch and PAM on the nodes
alt: A node resolves a user through nsswitch: local files, then the SSSD cache, and only on a miss a query to LDAP.
cap: A node checks local files, then the SSSD cache, and asks LDAP only when the cache has no answer.

name: h24-launch-lookups
title: Job launch on many nodes: who answers the user lookup
spec: Two side-by-side panels with titles. Left panel title: Each node asks the directory. A grid of many small node boxes, each labelled node, drawn compactly in three rows. One single arrow from the node grid container to a box at the right titled LDAP directory, labelled every node calls getpwnam() and initgroups() at task launch. Under the arrow, the note thousands of queries at the same moment. Orange highlight on this arrow and the note, labelled the single most important item: the lookup storm at job start. Right panel title: Slurm passes the answer down. A single box at the top labelled Slurm controller, with an arrow down to a grid of the same small node boxes, labelled passwd and group data sent with the job. Each node box inside has a small tag resolved locally. A note under the grid: verify support and semantics on your Slurm version. The right panel has no arrow to the LDAP directory, and a small grey note under the title: enable_nss_slurm in LaunchParameters. Keep the two panels separate with a vertical divider. No takeaway bar.
alt: Without enable_nss_slurm, every node queries LDAP at job start; with it, the controller passes the user data down.
cap: Each compute node normally queries the directory at job start, but enable_nss_slurm lets the controller pass the user data down instead.

name: h24-offboard-order
title: Offboarding in order: close the front door first
spec: A top-to-bottom sequence of five numbered step cards, number circles 1 to 5 in time order, each card a wide horizontal box with a title and a one-line label, and a thin arrow linking each card to the next. Step 1, title: Disable LDAP login. Label: lock the account first, so nothing new can start. Icon: a lock. Step 2, title: Zero or remove Slurm associations. Label: set the sacctmgr limits to zero or remove the associations, and keep the accounting history. Icon: a ledger or a book. Step 3, title: Reassign or archive files. Label: move or archive the user's files, as the policy says. Icon: a folder with an arrow. Step 4, title: Remove SSH keys and revoke tokens. Label: remove the SSH keys, then revoke tokens such as API keys, registry tokens, object store keys and Slurm REST JWTs. Icon: a key with a cross. Step 5, title: Disable cloud and Kubernetes access. Label: the last door to close. Icon: a cloud. A grey side note beside step 2: never delete historical job records. A grey side note beside step 4: the last step is usually the one that leaves a token alive. Orange highlight on step 1, labelled the single most important item: lock the front door first, so every later step starts from a known state. No takeaway bar.
alt: Offboarding order: disable LDAP login, zero Slurm associations, reassign files, remove keys and tokens, then disable cloud access.
cap: Offboarding works best in a fixed order that closes the login path first and keeps the Slurm accounting history.

name: h25-proxyjump-hop
title: ProxyJump passes the connection through the bastion
spec: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel titled ProxyJump (ssh -J), the recommended choice. Three boxes in a row: Laptop (holds the private keys, labelled keys stay on the laptop), Bastion (labelled jump host, passes the encrypted connection through), login (labelled login.cluster.internal). Arrows run left to right from Laptop to Bastion to login. Under the arrow to login, a monospace label reads ssh -J user@bastion user@login. A bracket spans from Laptop to login with the text end to end encrypted. Right panel titled ForwardAgent yes (ssh -A), marked to avoid. Same three boxes, but the Bastion box holds an agent socket icon with a warning mark, and the label reads root on the intermediate host can use the agent socket. Orange note on the right panel: this exposes the user's agent socket to root on intermediate hosts. Keep the two panels equal in size, separated by a vertical divider. No green takeaway bar.
alt: ProxyJump sends an encrypted SSH connection through the bastion while keys stay on the laptop, unlike agent forwarding.
cap: ProxyJump passes an end-to-end encrypted connection through the bastion and keeps your keys on the laptop.

name: h25-x11-role-swap
title: The X11 role swap: the workstation is the server
spec: Two large boxes side by side with an arrow between them. Left box titled Your workstation, containing a monitor icon and the label X server, with the sub-labels owns the physical or virtual display, display :0, keyboard, mouse. Right box titled Cluster node, containing a window icon and the label X client, with the sub-label graphical application, for example xclock. An arrow runs from the X client in the cluster node box to the X server in the workstation box, labelled X protocol over UNIX domain or TCP sockets. Monospace commands under the X server box: xclock -display :0 and export DISPLAY=:0. Above the two boxes, a small note: the program is the client, the workstation is the server. Orange note on the arrow or the server box: the role is swapped, so workstation security matters too. No numbered steps, no green takeaway bar.
anchor: ### X11 and graphical tools (*Supercomputers for Linux Sysadmins* Chapter 18)
alt: In X11 the X server runs on the user's workstation and the graphical program on the cluster is the X client.
cap: In X11 the workstation runs the X server and the program running on the cluster is the client.

name: h25-ood-request-chain
title: How an Open OnDemand request reaches the compute node
spec: A left-to-right chain of four boxes with numbered step circles 1 to 4 above them. Box 1: User browser (monitor icon), arrow labelled HTTPS 443 to box 2. Box 2: Apache front end (gear or server icon), with the label authenticates the user. Arrow labelled reverse proxies each user to her PUN via Unix domain sockets to box 3. Box 3: Per-User NGINX (PUN), with the sub-label runs as the user, starts per-user NGINX processes (PUNs). Ruby and Node web apps are shown inside as a small note, and the label job submission and interactive apps. Arrow labelled reverse proxies to interactive apps via TCP sockets runs from Apache (box 2) down to box 4. Box 4, placed below box 3 in the lower right: Compute node, containing the interactive apps labelled RStudio, Jupyter and VNC desktop. The Apache to compute node arrow must not cross the PUN arrow. Orange highlight on the PUN box: it runs as the user, so file access follows the user's real permissions. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Open OnDemand's Apache checks the user, hands traffic to that user's PUN, and proxies interactive apps on compute nodes over TCP.
cap: Open OnDemand's Apache authenticates you, passes your traffic to your own PUN, and proxies interactive apps on compute nodes.

name: h26-trap-pipeline
title: How an SNMP trap reaches your handler script
spec: Left-to-right flow with four numbered step circles (1 to 4) above boxes. Box 1: Switch, PDU or UPS (device icon) with the label sends Trap, and a note UDP port 162 on the arrow to box 2. Box 2: snmptrapd (manager, monitoring server icon), with a small monospace line authCommunity log,execute,net public inside the box. Arrow labelled traphandle NET-SNMP-EXAMPLES-MIB::netSnmpExampleHeartbeatNotification runs to box 3. Box 3: Handler script (script icon) with the monospace label /tmp/demo, and a note production should use a non-/tmp path. Arrow from box 3 to box 4. Box 4: a document icon with the monospace label trap log line written to a log file, shown as /tmp/demo.log. Below box 3, a separate panel titled stdin lines, containing three stacked rows: line 1 sender hostname, line 2 sender IP and transport, then oid val pairs one per line after that. The arrow from snmptrapd to the handler is labelled with stdin. Orange highlight on box 2 with the note a community mismatch drops the trap before the handler runs. No green takeaway bar.
alt: A device trap reaches snmptrapd, which checks the community and runs a handler that reads the sender and variables from standard input.
cap: A trap goes from the device to snmptrapd, which checks the community and then runs your handler script with the trap details on standard input.

name: h26-ups-shutdown-order
title: Who shuts down first when the power goes out
spec: A horizontal timeline arrow across the top, left to right, with four numbered step circles (1 to 4) on it. Marker 1: Grid outage (lightning or plug icon). Marker 2 below the timeline: UPS carries the load for at least 10 to 30 minutes (battery icon). Marker 3: 5 minutes without utility power, labelled controlled cluster shutdown starts, with the text that prohibits new jobs. Marker 4 at the far right: the final stage. Below the timeline, two lanes of boxes in order. Lane 1 box, placed first, labelled Compute nodes stop first, with the tag upsmon slave (shut down first). Lane 2 box, placed last, labelled Network file systems and monitoring servers, with the tag upsmon master (shut down last, attached to the UPS). An arrow runs from the Compute nodes box to the Network file systems box. Orange highlight on the arrow or the upsmon master box: the master shuts down last. No green takeaway bar.
anchor: ### UPS monitoring with Network UPS Tools (`NUT`) and `apcupsd`
alt: On a grid outage the UPS carries the load, then compute nodes shut down first and file systems and monitoring shut down last.
cap: During a long outage the compute nodes shut down first, and the file systems and monitoring servers shut down last.

name: h26-alert-decision
title: Decide between a page, a ticket and a graph
spec: A top-down decision flow. Start box at top: Symptom seen, with a bell icon. Diamond or rounded question box: needs human action? Two exits. Yes branch goes right to a box PAGE, shown as an orange-highlighted box with an alarm icon, with example text: rack where 40 percent of GPUs show Xid 79. No branch goes down to a second question box: degradation? Yes branch goes right to box TICKET (clipboard icon), with the label degradations. No branch goes down to box GRAPH (chart icon), with example text: GPU at 99 C might be fine for a minute. Below the PAGE box, a small note: every paged alert needs a runbook. Above the flow, a one-line title in the diagram: alert on symptoms that need human action; graph everything else. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: A symptom becomes a page if it needs immediate human action, a ticket if it is a degradation, and otherwise just a graph.
cap: A symptom pages someone only when it needs immediate human action, becomes a ticket when it is a degradation, and otherwise stays on a graph.

name: h26-util-vs-tensor
title: GPU_UTIL can read 99 percent while the tensor cores sit idle
spec: Three horizontal meter bars stacked vertically, each with a full track of 100 percent and a green fill for its value. Bar 1 labelled DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL, sub-label a kernel was running, value 99 percent, filled almost fully. Bar 2 labelled DCGM_FI_PROF_PIPE_TENSOR_ACTIVE, sub-label Tensor Cores busy, value 4 percent, short fill. Bar 3 labelled DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE, sub-label HBM memory interface busy, value 82 percent, long fill. Orange highlight on Bar 2, the short tensor bar, with the note tensor cores idle. Beside Bar 3, a note: high DRAM with low tensor means memory-bound. A small caption at the bottom with the example labels: 64-GPU job, H100 GPUs draw 260 W of a possible 700 W. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: A job can show 99 percent GPU utilisation while its tensor activity is 4 percent and DRAM activity is 82 percent.
cap: GPU utilisation alone can show 99 percent while the tensor cores are nearly idle, so check the profiling fields too.

name: h27-snapshot-vs-backup
title: Snapshots and mirrors share the failure domain, a backup does not
spec: Three side-by-side panels separated by thin dividers, each headed by a name. Panel 1 titled Snapshot: a storage array box containing two items, Live data and Snapshot, both inside the same outline, with a label same array and same admin credentials across the box. A small note: deleted together. Panel 2 titled Replication (mirror): a Primary box on the left and a Mirror box on the right, with one arrow from Primary to Mirror labelled deletions and corruption copied. A note: the mirror deletes it too. Panel 3 titled Backup: a Primary box on the left and, separated by a dashed line that marks a separate system, a Backup copy box on the right, labelled immutable or offline copy. Each panel has an icon: a camera for snapshot, two disks for mirror, a locked box for backup. Orange highlight on Panel 3 (backup) as the only copy that survives a bad change. Keep text at least 24 px. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Snapshots and mirrors sit in the same failure domain as the live data and copy deletions, while a separate backup survives a bad change.
cap: A snapshot or mirror lives in the same failure domain as the data and copies deletions too, so only a separate backup protects against a bad change.

name: h27-link-dest-snapshots
title: Hard links make a second snapshot cost only its changes
spec: Two snapshot folder boxes side by side, left labelled snaps/day1 and right labelled snaps/day2. Inside snaps/day1, file boxes f1.bin and f7.bin, with a size note of 200 files, 4,004 KB in total. Inside snaps/day2, file boxes f1.bin and f7.bin. An arrow from day1 f1.bin to day2 f1.bin, labelled same inode (hard link, no extra space). The day2 f7.bin box is drawn new and highlighted, labelled new inode, modified file. A monospace command above the arrow between the boxes: rsync -a --delete --link-dest=$PWD/snaps/day1 data/ snaps/day2/. Under the day2 box, a sum block: first snapshot 4,004 KB, plus changes 24 KB, equals 4,028 KB together. Orange highlight on the new f7.bin box. Numbered steps: 1 for the first snapshot run, 2 for the second run. No green takeaway bar.
anchor: ### rsync, batch updates, and hard-link snapshots
alt: A second rsync snapshot hard-links the unchanged file to the first snapshot and only the modified file takes new space.
cap: A second rsync snapshot hard-links unchanged files to the first, so it only takes new space for the files that changed.

name: h27-dr-restore-order
title: Restore the control plane in dependency order
spec: A vertical stack of six numbered boxes, top to bottom, connected by downward arrows, with a step number circle beside each box. Box 1: Identity (key icon). Box 2: DNS (globe icon). Box 3: Provisioning (server rack icon). Box 4: Storage (disk cylinder icon). Box 5: Scheduler (clock or gear icon). Box 6: Users (person icon). Between box 5 and box 6 the arrow is the only one labelled then users. A thin side note on the left reads each layer depends on the one before it. Orange highlight on box 1 with the note restore first, since everything depends on it. No green takeaway bar. Keep the stack compact with equal spacing.
alt: A full recovery restores identity, DNS, provisioning, storage, scheduler and then users, each layer depending on the one before.
cap: Restore identity first, then DNS, provisioning, storage and the scheduler, and bring users back last.

name: h27-restore-test-tiers
title: Three levels of restore testing, from daily to quarterly
spec: A three-step staircase rising from bottom-left to top-right. Step 1 at the bottom left, labelled Level 1, with the tag daily, the text automated restore of a random file, and a note checksum compare. Step 2 in the middle, labelled Level 2, with the tag weekly, the text restore of a database dump into a scratch instance, and a note followed by a smoke query. Step 3 at the top right, labelled Level 3, with the tag quarterly, the text full-system recovery drill. Arrows run up the staircase from Step 1 to Step 2 to Step 3. Each step has a small icon: a file with a check mark, a database cylinder, a full server rack. Orange highlight on Step 3 as the most complete test. Below the staircase, a single line of text: each level proves a bigger part of the restore. No numbered step circles beyond the level labels. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Restore testing has three levels: a daily random file restore with checksum, a weekly database restore with a smoke query, and a quarterly full recovery drill.
cap: Restore testing has three levels, from a daily file restore with a checksum to a quarterly full-system recovery drill.

name: h28-bonnie-layers
title: Where bonnie++ really wrote: the page cache, not the disk
spec: A vertical stack of three layer boxes connected by downward arrows, with numbered step circles 1 to 3 beside them. Top box 1: bonnie++ Per Chr test, with the sub-label one-byte writes and the reported figure 739 Kbytes/sec at 99% CPU. A monospace note under it: write(3, "6", 1) = 1 and no fsync(2). Arrow down labelled one-byte vfs_write() calls. Middle box 2: OS page cache, with the sub-label 1,176,936 one-byte vfs_write() calls, and a small note: cachestat 1 shows 100.00% page-cache hits and dirties. Arrow down, drawn dashed, to box 3. Bottom box 3: Disk, drawn grey and empty, with the label 0 disk IOPS from iostat -sxz 1 and the note no block_rq_issue events. Side tags on the right of each box name the tool that showed it: strace for box 1, bpftrace and cachestat for box 2, iostat and bpftrace for box 3. Orange highlight on box 3, the layer the test never reached. A green panel on the left is not needed. No green takeaway bar.
alt: bonnie++ made a million one-byte writes into the page cache, and no disk I/O happened, so the test measured memory.
cap: The bonnie++ test made about a million one-byte writes into the page cache and never reached the disk.

name: h28-acceptance-order
title: Cluster acceptance runs in eight ordered stages
spec: Eight numbered boxes arranged in a snake path, four per row, left to right on the top row and right to left on the bottom row, with arrows between consecutive boxes. Each box has a number circle (r=24, green, white number) and an icon beside its title. Box 1: Inventory and firmware audit (chip icon), sub-label BIOS, BMC, NIC and GPU firmware match the baseline. Box 2: Burn in the hardware (flame or thermometer icon), sub-label 24 to 72 hours, watch for errors and thermal throttling. Box 3: Per-node performance (gauge icon), sub-label compare each node with the peer median, flag any node below 95 percent of the median. Box 4: Validate the fabric (network icon), sub-label ib_write_bw and ib_send_lat, then nccl-tests at scale. Box 5: Validate storage (disk cylinder icon), sub-label IOR, mdtest and fio. Box 6: Run the system end to end (server rack icon), sub-label full-cluster HPL, then a multi-day training-like job. Box 7: Smoke-test the scheduler and software (gear icon), sub-label Slurm, containers, identity and monitoring. Box 8: Document the results (document icon), sub-label sign off before each payment milestone. Orange highlight on box 2, where infant mortality shows up. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Acceptance testing runs eight stages in order, from inventory and burn-in through fabric, storage and end-to-end tests to signed-off documentation.
cap: Acceptance testing runs in eight ordered stages, starting with inventory and burn-in and ending with signed documentation.

name: h28-batch-halving
title: Halve the batch size to tell a network-bound job from a compute-bound one
spec: Top-down decision flow. Start box at top: DDP gradient all_reduce at 60 GB/s on a 100 GB/s NIC, with a note the gradient payload stays fixed when the batch size changes. Step number circle 1 beside an arrow down labelled halve the batch size. Diamond or question box: does NIC throughput stay at 60 GB/s? Two exits. Left exit, labelled yes, leads to a green box: stays at 60 GB/s, so the network is the bottleneck, result communication-bound. Right exit, labelled no, leads to a second box: drops to 40 GB/s, so the GPUs are not finishing compute fast enough to keep the NIC busy, result compute-bound. Below both results, step number circle 2 with the box double the batch size as a reverse check, with two notes: a communication-bound job keeps the NIC pinned at 60 GB/s, and a compute-bound job spends a shrinking share of each iteration in all_reduce. Orange highlight on the communication-bound result box. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Halving the batch size shows whether the NIC stays pinned at 60 GB/s, which means communication-bound, or drops to 40 GB/s, which means compute-bound.
cap: Halving the batch size tells you whether the NIC stays pinned, which means the job is communication-bound, or drops, which means it is compute-bound.

name: h29-mpi-models
title: Hybrid MPI carries its own MPI, bind MPI borrows the host's
spec: Two side-by-side panels separated by a vertical divider. Left panel titled Hybrid model. Top row: a box labelled Host launcher (srun or mpirun, with the sub-label host MPI). Below it, a box labelled Container, holding a box labelled container MPI, with the note PMIx compatible with the host. An arrow from the host launcher down to the container, labelled starts apptainer exec per rank. A monospace note under the panel: srun --mpi=pmix apptainer exec --nv --cleanenv -B /scratch:/scratch myenv.sif python train.py. Right panel titled Bind model. Top row: the same Host launcher box with host MPI. Below it, a container box with no MPI inside, and an arrow from a box labelled Host MPI libraries into the container, labelled bind-mounted with -B. A note: admins must allow user bind mounts. Under both panels, a two-row comparison strip with labels: Self-contained, portable (hybrid) versus exact host MPI match, tied to that cluster paths (bind). Orange highlight on the bind model's Host MPI libraries arrow. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: In the hybrid model the container carries its own MPI, while in the bind model the host MPI libraries are mounted into a container that has none.
cap: The hybrid model ships MPI inside the container, while the bind model mounts the host's MPI libraries into a container that has none.

name: h29-glibc-mismatch
title: Why --nv fails when the container's glibc is too old
spec: Left-to-right flow with three boxes and arrows. Box 1 on the left: Host OS, Ubuntu 24.04 with glibc 2.39 (chip icon), with the note GPU node. Box 2 in the middle: Host NVIDIA driver libraries, libcuda.so and libnvidia-ml.so, labelled bind-mounted by --nv. An arrow from Box 1 to Box 2 labelled compiled against the host glibc. Box 3 on the right: Container, Ubuntu 18.04 with glibc 2.27 (box icon). An arrow from Box 2 to Box 3 labelled injected into the container. Below the arrow into Box 3, a red-free warning in orange: GLIBC_2.34 not found (required by libcuda.so.1). Under Box 3 a note: rebase onto a base whose glibc is at least as new as the host. Monospace command above Box 2: apptainer exec --nv old.sif nvidia-smi. Orange highlight on the error message. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: The --nv flag injects host libcuda built against a newer glibc, so an older container image fails with a GLIBC_2.34 not found error.
cap: The --nv flag injects host driver libraries built against a newer glibc, so an older container image fails with a GLIBC_2.34 not found error.

name: h29-repro-levels
title: Four levels of reproducibility, each asking more of the process
spec: A four-step staircase rising from bottom-left to top-right, with step number circles 1 to 4 on the treads. Step 1 at the bottom: Rerun, sub-label the same image, depends on immutability. Step 2: Rebuild, sub-label the same image from the same recipe, depends on a deterministic build. Step 3: Reuse, sub-label the environment on another system, depends on portability. Step 4 at the top: Understand, sub-label what is inside and where it came from, depends on provenance and metadata. Each step has a small icon: a lock for rerun, a hammer for rebuild, a plug for reuse, a magnifying glass for understand. Arrows run up the staircase from step 1 to step 4. Side note on the right: most teams aim for the first two levels and make the last two possible. Orange highlight on step 4, the level that needs provenance. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Reproducibility has four levels, rerun, rebuild, reuse and understand, and each level depends on a different property.
cap: Reproducibility has four levels, from rerunning the same image to understanding what is inside it, and each one needs more of the process.

name: h30-staged-shutdown
title: The staged shutdown: six stages, each giving up something to save something else
spec: A horizontal timeline arrow across the middle, left to right, with six numbered step circles (r=24, green, white number) placed on it. Above the timeline at the left, a start marker labelled Power fails, with the note apcupsd runs onbattery and starts haltall. Stage 1 box above the timeline: Log the event and warn users, monospace wall. Stage 2 box below the timeline: Wait 30 minutes, with a branch arrow down to a small box labelled power returns, offbattery ends haltall. Stage 3 box: Power off the idle nodes, found by checking each node's load. Stage 4 box: Poll the UPS TIMELEFT value every minute until 5 minutes of battery remain. Stage 5 box: Stop the batch queue and cancel running jobs, monospace scontrol and scancel, then wait a minute. Stage 6 box at the far right: Power off all remaining compute nodes, then power off the head node. Each stage box has a one-line cost tag underneath in italic: stage 2 gives up time to ride through a brief outage; stage 3 gives up the idle nodes to save power for the busy ones; stage 5 gives up the running jobs to save the file system and hardware. Orange highlight on stage 5, the most costly step. Icons: a bell for stage 1, a clock for stage 2, a power plug for stage 3, a battery for stage 4, a stop sign for stage 5, a server rack for stage 6. No green takeaway bar.
alt: A staged cluster shutdown logs and warns, waits 30 minutes, powers off idle nodes, polls battery time, cancels jobs and then powers off the rest.
cap: A staged shutdown warns users, waits, powers off idle nodes, cancels jobs at five minutes of battery, and only then powers off the rest.

name: h30-psu-feed-designs
title: Interleaved feeds crash every server; separate feeds lose only half
spec: Two side-by-side panels separated by a vertical divider. Left panel titled Interleaved dual sources, with a red-free orange STOP label at the top. Two UPS boxes at the top: UPS A and UPS B. Under them, one server box containing six PSU boxes in a row, the first three linked to UPS A and the last three to UPS B, with thin lines. A callout on UPS A marked failure, and a note under the server: 3 PSUs lost, 5 of 6 rule broken, the server shuts down. Mark the server with a large X. Right panel titled N with two separate sources. Two UPS boxes at the top, UPS A and UPS B. Below them, two rows of server boxes: the top row of servers fed only from UPS A (all 6 cords), the bottom row fed only from UPS B (all 6 cords). A callout on UPS A failure marked affects only half the servers, and the bottom row stays green and running. Orange highlight on the failed UPS A in the right panel is not needed, use the left-panel X as the only orange element. Under the panels, a single line of text: the usual redundancy model assumes two feeds, but the server's own 5-of-6 PSUs change the answer. No green takeaway bar.
anchor: ### 3.2 Redundancy: why servers with internal power supplies need care
alt: Interleaving three PSUs on each of two UPS sources takes every server down when one UPS fails, while splitting whole servers across UPS sources loses only half.
cap: Wiring three power supplies to each of two UPS sources takes every server down if one UPS fails, but giving each source whole servers loses only half.

name: h30-cold-plate-loop
title: Cold plates carry heat from the chips to a CDU, which passes it to facility water
spec: A left-to-right loop diagram with four boxes and arrows. Box 1 on the left: Cold plates, drawn as a flat plate on a chip, with two sub-labels CPU and GPU. Arrow from Box 1 to Box 2 labelled warm liquid. Box 2 in the middle: CDU (coolant distribution unit, pump and box icon), with the sub-label pumps coolant around the loop. Arrow from Box 2 to Box 3 labelled heat passed to facility water. Box 3 on the right: Heat exchanger, with the label facility water loop. A return arrow runs from Box 2 back to Box 1 along the top, labelled coolant around the loop. A small sensor box with a drop icon labelled leak detection sits under the loop, attached by a dotted line to Box 1. Orange highlight on the cold plate box. Pipes drawn as thick lines in light green. Air-cooled parts shown as a small fan icon with the label fans cool the lower-power parts, placed under Box 1. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Cold plates on the CPUs and GPUs send warm liquid to a CDU, which pumps coolant around the loop and passes the heat to facility water.
cap: Cold plates on the chips send warm liquid to a CDU, which pumps coolant around the loop and passes the heat to facility water.

name: h31-build-order
title: Build a GPU cluster from the bottom up, one layer at a time
spec: An ascending staircase of eight stacked layer boxes, drawn from bottom-left (layer 1) to top-right (layer 8), each box a step up from the one below, with an upward arrow along the staircase edge labelled build order, bottom to top. Each box has a number circle (r=24, green, white number) and an icon beside its title. Layer 1: Facility power and cooling (lightning-bolt icon), sub-label check the rack power budget before the chassis goes in. Layer 2: Out-of-band and in-band networks (network icon), sub-label BMC to the OOB switch, host NICs to the in-band switch. Layer 3: Bare-metal provisioning (server icon), sub-label DHCP and TFTP from nodes.csv, then a golden image. Layer 4: Identity (key or badge icon), sub-label LDAP or FreeIPA with SSSD, UIDs and GIDs match on every node. Layer 5: Fabrics and parallel storage (disk cylinder icon), sub-label Subnet Manager, ibdiagnet, then mount the parallel filesystem. Layer 6: Scheduler and cgroup isolation (gear icon), sub-label slurm.conf, gres.conf and cgroup.conf generated from hardware.csv. Layer 7: Acceptance gates and burn-in (gauge icon), sub-label NHC, HPL, IOR and a 24 to 72 hour burn-in. Layer 8: Telemetry, alerting and backup (chart icon), sub-label Prometheus scraping, alert rules checked, backups verified. Orange highlight on layer 6 with a small tag: rookie mistake, Slurm installed on day one before identity and storage. No green takeaway bar.
alt: A new GPU cluster is built in eight layers from facility power up to telemetry and backup, with each layer depending on the one below it.
cap: A new GPU cluster is built in eight layers, from facility power at the bottom to telemetry and backup at the top, and each layer depends on the one below.

name: h31-single-source-pipeline
title: One inventory in, every config out
spec: Left-to-right flow with three columns: inputs on the left, generators in the middle, outputs on the right. Four input boxes stacked vertically on the left, each with a file icon: hardware.csv (sub-label machines), nodes.csv (sub-label how each machine boots), users.csv (sub-label who may use the cluster), train.sbatch (sub-label a researcher's job script). Note inside a container around the three CSV inputs: all live in Git. Four generator boxes in the middle column, aligned with their inputs: gen_slurm_conf.py, gen_provision.py, identity_gen.py, sbatch_lint.py. Output boxes on the right: a container labelled slurm/ holding slurm.conf, gres.conf and cgroup.conf, with an arrow from gen_slurm_conf.py to that container; a box provision/dnsmasq.conf and iPXE scripts for gen_provision.py; a box identity/ holding users.ldif, sacctmgr.sh and mkhomes.sh for identity_gen.py; and for sbatch_lint.py an output box labelled no findings. From the slurm/ container, one arrow to a check box slurmconf_lint.py. Orange highlight on the hardware.csv input, the single row that updates every subsystem. Keep arrows orthogonal and avoid crossings. No numbered steps. No green takeaway bar.
alt: Each inventory file feeds one generator, and the generators write the Slurm, DHCP, identity and job-check outputs.
cap: Each inventory file feeds one generator, and together they write every scheduler, boot and identity config from one source of truth.

name: h31-acceptance-gates
title: Ten acceptance gates, ordered from cheapest to most expensive
spec: Ten numbered boxes in a snake path: gates 1 to 5 in a top row from left to right, then gates 6 to 10 in a bottom row from right to left, with arrows between consecutive gates, so the path reads in order. Each box has a number circle (r=24, green, white number) and an icon: gate 1 a thermometer, gate 2 a chip, gate 3 a key, gate 4 a single server, gate 5 a link between GPUs, gate 6 a network switch, gate 7 a disk cylinder, gate 8 a clock or queue, gate 9 a quota gauge, gate 10 a flame for burn-in. Box labels: 1 Out-of-Band and Sensors; 2 Host Health and PCIe/NVLink; 3 Cluster Identity and MUNGE; 4 Single-Node GPU and Memory; 5 Intra-Node NVLink Collectives; 6 Inter-Node RDMA Fabric; 7 Parallel Storage I/O; 8 Scheduler and cgroup Isolation; 9 Policy and Quota Enforcement; 10 Fault Injection and 72h Burn-In. Above the row a thin arrow labelled cheapest to most expensive, left to right on top and reversed on the bottom. Orange highlight on gate 10. No green takeaway bar.
anchor: ## 4. Ten-gate acceptance testing and burn-in protocol
alt: The ten acceptance gates run from out-of-band sensors through identity, GPU, network, storage and scheduler checks to a 72-hour fault-injection burn-in.
cap: The ten acceptance gates run from cheap out-of-band checks to a 72-hour burn-in, and each gate assumes the ones before it have passed.

name: h31-drill-recovery-loop
title: Drill 1: from a dropped GPU back to service
spec: A horizontal loop of five boxes with arrows between them in order, numbered 1 to 5 with number circles, then a return arrow from box 5 back to a final state box labelled State=RESUME. Box 1: Dropped GPU, with a monospace note Xid 79, GPU has fallen off the bus, and a warning icon. Box 2: Epilog or NHC exits non-zero. Box 3: Drain the node with a reason and a ticket, monospace scontrol update NodeName=gpu003 State=DRAIN Reason=NHC GPU count 7/8 Xid 79 ticket INC-1042. Box 4: Cold power cycle through Redfish (ForceOff and On), or an RMA replacement, shown as two alternative small sub-boxes joined by or. Box 5: Re-run Gate 2 and Gate 5, the GPU health and single-node collective checks. Final box: State=RESUME, with a check icon. Orange highlight on box 3, the drain step that records why the node is out. No green takeaway bar.
anchor: ## 5. Day-2 operations drills: practicing the bad day
alt: A dropped GPU makes the node exit its check, get drained with a ticket, be power cycled or replaced, pass gates 2 and 5, and return to service.
cap: A dropped GPU drains its node with a ticket, then the node is power cycled or replaced, re-checked, and only then resumed.
